questions.q: A structural causal model over $\{Z,X,Y\}$ has equations $Z:=U_Z$, $X:=f_X(Z,U_X)$, $Y:=f_Y(X,Z,U_Y)$ with the exogenous $U_Z,U_X,U_Y$ mutually independent. Which observational factorization does it entail?
choices: $p(z,x,y)=p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x,z)$
$p(z,x,y)=p(x)\,p(z\mid x)\,p(y\mid z)$
$p(z,x,y)=p(z\mid x,y)\,p(x\mid y)\,p(y)$
questions.explain: Each structural equation $X_i:=f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i,U_i)$ with independent noise induces the conditional $p(x_i\mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$, and the DAG factorizes the joint as $\prod_i p(x_i\mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ — exactly the Bayes-net factorization. Here $Z$ has no parents, $X$ has parent $Z$, and $Y$ has parents $\{X,Z\}$, giving $p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x,z)$.

questions.q: Two different SCMs can entail the very same observational distribution $p(x)$ yet disagree about interventions. What does this tell you?
choices: The observational joint alone does not determine causal effects; the structural equations (the arrows) carry information beyond $p(x)$
One of the two SCMs must be wrong
Interventions are always determined by $p(x)$
The two SCMs must have the same DAG
questions.explain: An SCM commits to more than the joint it entails: the directed equations say which variable responds to which under intervention. Markov-equivalent DAGs (e.g. $X\to Y$ vs $X\leftarrow Y$) can give identical $p(x,y)$ but opposite answers to $\operatorname{do}(X)$. This is why causal questions need a causal model, not just a fitted distribution.

questions.q: An SCM over four binary variables has DAG $Z\to X\to Y$ and $Z\to Y$. Counting one free parameter per parent configuration of each binary node, how many free parameters does the entailed factorization $p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x,z)$ have?
questions.explain: $p(z)$ needs $1$; $p(x\mid z)$ needs one per value of $z$, so $2$; $p(y\mid x,z)$ needs one per $(x,z)$ pair, so $2^2=4$. Total $1+2+4=7$, versus $2^3-1=7$ for the full joint here — but the structure still pins down the causal direction the raw table cannot.

questions.q: What does the intervention $\operatorname{do}(X=x)$ do to the causal graph?
choices: Deletes all arrows pointing into $X$ and sets $X=x$, leaving every other equation untouched
Deletes all arrows pointing out of $X$
Conditions on $X=x$ without changing the graph
Removes the node $X$ from the graph entirely
questions.explain: $\operatorname{do}(X=x)$ is graph surgery (mutilation): cut the incoming arrows so $X$ no longer listens to its old causes, clamp $X=x$, and keep all other structural equations as they were. The arrows out of $X$ stay — that is how the intervention propagates downstream to $Y$.

questions.q: In a confounded graph $X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y$ with $X\rightarrow Y$, why does $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ generally differ from $p(y\mid x)$?
choices: Conditioning on $X=x$ also reweights $Z$ through the backdoor $X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y$; surgery cuts $X\leftarrow Z$ so $Z$ keeps its original distribution
The do-operator changes the value of $Y$ directly
They never differ — conditioning and intervening are the same
Because $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ ignores the edge $X\to Y$
questions.explain: Observing $X=x$ tells you about $Z$ via the backdoor path, so $p(y\mid x)$ mixes the causal effect with $Z$-driven association. Intervening deletes $X\leftarrow Z$, so $Z$ is no longer informed by $X$ and retains its marginal $p(z)$ — the truncated factorization $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))=\sum_z p(y\mid x,z)\,p(z)$. The two agree only when no such backdoor (confounding) exists.

questions.q: Order the steps for computing $p(v\mid \operatorname{do}(X=x))$ from an SCM via the truncated factorization.
items: Delete the factor $p(x\mid \mathrm{pa}_X)$ for the intervened node $X$
Read off $p(v\mid \operatorname{do}(x))=\prod_{i:\,V_i\neq X} p(v_i\mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ evaluated at $X=x$
questions.explain: The g-formula drops exactly the mechanism of the intervened variable (its arrows-in are cut) and evaluates the remaining product at the clamped value. Everything else — the noise distributions and the other structural conditionals — is untouched, which is what makes the interventional law differ from the observational conditional.

questions.q: A set $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion relative to $(X,Y)$ if:
choices: $Z$ blocks every backdoor path from $X$ to $Y$ and no node in $Z$ is a descendant of $X$
$Z$ contains every variable in the graph
$Z$ blocks the direct path $X\to Y$
$Z$ is a descendant of $X$ that mediates the effect
questions.explain: The backdoor criterion has two clauses: (1) $Z$ blocks all paths from $X$ to $Y$ that start with an arrow into $X$ (the backdoor, confounding paths), and (2) $Z$ includes no descendant of $X$ — adjusting for a descendant can reopen paths or block part of the very effect you want. When both hold, $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))=\sum_z p(y\mid x,z)\,p(z)$.

questions.q: Simpson's paradox. A drug is given more often to a sicker group. Among the LOW-risk stratum, recovery is $0.93$ on drug vs $0.87$ on placebo; among the HIGH-risk stratum, $0.73$ on drug vs $0.69$ on placebo — the drug helps in BOTH strata. The within-stratum (adjusted) treatment effect for the high-risk group is $0.73-0.69$. Enter that number.
questions.explain: The correct, confounder-adjusted effect compares treated vs untreated WITHIN a stratum of the confounder $Z$ (risk): $0.73-0.69=0.04$ for the high-risk group (and $0.93-0.87=0.06$ for the low-risk group). Both are positive. Simpson's paradox is that the AGGREGATE rates can reverse this — pooling lets the drug look worse because it was preferentially given to the high-risk group, who recover less for reasons that have nothing to do with the drug. Adjusting for $Z$ recovers the truth.

questions.q: On the confounded graph $X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y$, $X\rightarrow Y$, with $Z$ observed, what does the adjustment formula $\sum_z p(y\mid x,z)\,p(z)$ compute?
choices: $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ — the genuine causal effect, with the $Z$-confounding removed
$p(y\mid x)$ — the naive observational conditional
$p(x\mid y)$ — the reversed conditional
$p(z\mid x,y)$ — the posterior over the confounder
questions.explain: Because $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion here (it blocks the single backdoor path $X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y$ and is not a descendant of $X$), the adjustment formula equals the interventional distribution $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$. Note the weight is the marginal $p(z)$, not $p(z\mid x)$: surgery on $X$ leaves $Z$ at its original distribution.

questions.q: What does it mean for a causal effect $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ to be 'identifiable' from a causal graph?
choices: It can be written entirely in terms of the observational distribution $p$ — computable from data without running the experiment
It can be estimated only by performing a randomized trial
The graph contains no unobserved variables
The effect equals the observational conditional $p(y\mid x)$
questions.explain: Identifiability is a graph-theoretic property: the interventional quantity can be reduced, using the rules of do-calculus, to an expression in the observational distribution alone. If it is identifiable you can compute it from passively collected data; if not, no amount of observational data suffices and you genuinely need an experiment or extra assumptions.

questions.q: The front-door criterion identifies $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ in the graph $X\to M\to Y$ with an UNOBSERVED confounder $U$ pointing into both $X$ and $Y$. Why can the backdoor adjustment NOT be used here, but the front-door formula can?
choices: The backdoor path $X\leftarrow U\rightarrow Y$ cannot be blocked because $U$ is unobserved; the front-door formula instead chains the identifiable effects $X\to M$ and $M\to Y$ through the observed mediator $M$
There is no backdoor path in this graph
The mediator $M$ is a descendant of $U$
The front-door formula requires $U$ to be observed too
questions.explain: An admissible backdoor set would have to contain $U$ to block $X\leftarrow U\rightarrow Y$, but $U$ is unobserved, so no observed set works. The front-door route uses the mediator: $X\to M$ has no unblocked backdoor, and $M\to Y$ is identifiable adjusting for $X$. Composing them gives $p(y\mid \operatorname{do}(x))=\sum_m p(m\mid x)\sum_{x'} p(y\mid m,x')\,p(x')$.

questions.q: Which statements about Pearl's three rules of do-calculus are correct?
choices: They are complete for identifiability: if an effect is identifiable, repeated application of the three rules will derive a do-free expression
Rule 2 governs when an action $\operatorname{do}(z)$ can be exchanged for a mere observation of $z$
They let you delete a $\operatorname{do}$ term whenever there are no causal paths from that node to the outcome left in the mutilated graph
They can identify any effect even when crucial confounders are unobserved and the graph offers no front-door or backdoor route
questions.explain: Rule 1 handles inserting/deleting observations, Rule 2 the action/observation exchange, Rule 3 the insertion/deletion of actions; together they are sound and (Shpitser–Pearl) complete — failure to reduce to a do-free form means the effect is genuinely non-identifiable. The last option is false: some graphs (e.g. the 'bow arc' with an unobserved confounder directly on $X\to Y$ and no mediator) are provably non-identifiable.

questions.q: Order the three steps of computing a counterfactual $Y_{x'}$ on an SCM, given factual evidence $E$.
items: Abduction: update the distribution of the exogenous noise $U$ to $p(U\mid E)$ using the observed evidence
Action: apply $\operatorname{do}(X=x')$ to the SCM, replacing $X$'s equation by the constant $x'$
Prediction: compute the distribution of $Y$ in the modified model under the updated noise
questions.explain: Counterfactuals are the third rung. Abduction infers what the unobserved background factors $U$ must have been to produce the facts; the action surgically sets $X=x'$ on the SAME inferred world; prediction reads off $Y$. Crucially the noise is held at its posterior $p(U\mid E)$ throughout — that is what makes the query about the same individual rather than a fresh draw.

questions.q: Why is a counterfactual query strictly stronger than an interventional one — why can't $\operatorname{do}(X=x')$ alone answer 'would this particular patient have recovered had they taken the drug'?
choices: $\operatorname{do}(X=x')$ gives the population distribution under intervention; the counterfactual conditions on this individual's actual outcome by fixing their exogenous noise via abduction
They are identical — counterfactual and interventional queries always coincide
The do-operator cannot set $X$ to a value it never took
Counterfactuals ignore the structural equations
questions.explain: An intervention answers 'what happens on average if we set $X=x'$' over a fresh draw of the noise. A counterfactual answers 'what would have happened to THIS unit, whose noise we partly learn from the observed facts.' The abduction step ($p(U\mid E)$) is exactly the extra ingredient; without it you lose the individual-level information.

questions.q: In the Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes framework, the consistency rule states:
choices: $Y=Y_X$ — the observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment actually received
$Y_0=Y_1$ — the two potential outcomes are always equal
$Y=\mathbb{E}[Y_1]-\mathbb{E}[Y_0]$
$Y_x$ is independent of $X$ unconditionally
questions.explain: Consistency links the observed world to the counterfactual one: the realized $Y$ is the potential outcome corresponding to the treatment level the unit actually got, $Y=Y_X$. It is the bridge that lets potential-outcome assumptions (like ignorability) translate into statements about observable data, and it is exactly the 'prediction' output of abduction–action–prediction on an SCM.

questions.q: The average treatment effect (ATE) for a binary treatment is defined as:
choices: $\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y_1]-\mathbb{E}[Y_0]$, the contrast of potential outcomes averaged over the population
$\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X{=}1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X{=}0]$, always, with no assumptions
$\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y_1]\,/\,\mathbb{E}[Y_0]$
$\tau=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y{=}1]$
questions.explain: The ATE is the population-average difference between the two potential outcomes, $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]-\mathbb{E}[Y_0]$. The naive observed contrast $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X{=}1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X{=}0]$ equals it only under no confounding (e.g. randomization); in general the naive contrast is biased by the confounders that drive treatment assignment.

questions.q: What pair of assumptions licenses estimating the ATE from observational data by adjusting for covariates $Z$?
choices: Ignorability $\{Y_0,Y_1\}\perp X\mid Z$ (no unobserved confounding) and positivity $0 < e(z) < 1$ (overlap)
Only that the sample size is large
That treatment is binary and the outcome is continuous
That the propensity score $e(z)$ is exactly $0$ or $1$
questions.explain: Ignorability says that, within strata of $Z$, treatment is as-good-as-random with respect to the potential outcomes — this is what makes the within-stratum contrast causal. Positivity (overlap) requires every covariate profile to have a nonzero chance of either treatment, so the comparison is not extrapolated. Both are needed: ignorability without overlap leaves cells where the effect is unestimable; randomization secures both by design with $Z$ empty.

questions.q: The inverse-propensity-weighting (IPW) estimator $\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_1]=\frac1n\sum_i \frac{X_i Y_i}{e(Z_i)}$ removes confounding bias by:
choices: Reweighting treated units by the inverse of their propensity $e(Z_i)=P(X{=}1\mid Z_i)$, creating a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of $Z$
Discarding all treated units
Weighting each unit by its outcome $Y_i$
Setting every weight to $1$, i.e. the naive average
questions.explain: IPW upweights treated units that were unlikely to be treated (small $e(Z_i)$) and downweights those that were almost certain to be, undoing the confounder-driven imbalance in who got treatment. The reweighted sample behaves like a randomized one, so the weighted average estimates $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]$. Overlap (positivity) matters because tiny $e(Z_i)$ blow up the weights and the variance; doubly-robust estimators combine IPW with an outcome model to stay consistent if either is correct.
